name: Numbers
v: On the first day of the seventh month, gather as a sacred assembly. Do no ordinary work. This is your day to sound the trumpets.
Bring a burnt offering — a fragrance that pleases the LORD: one young bull, one ram, seven year-old lambs without flaw.
With them, the grain offering: fine flour mixed with oil — three-tenths of an ephah for the bull, two-tenths for the ram,
one-tenth for each of the seven lambs.
Add a male goat as a sin offering, to make atonement for you.

All of this stands alongside the monthly burnt offering with its grain, the daily burnt offering with its grain, and their drink offerings — each in the prescribed measure. A fragrance that pleases the LORD, a fire-offering to him.
On the tenth day of this seventh month, gather as a sacred assembly. Humble yourselves. Do no work at all.
Bring a burnt offering — a fragrance that pleases the LORD: one young bull, one ram, seven year-old lambs without flaw. They must be unblemished.
With them, the grain offering: fine flour mixed with oil — three-tenths of an ephah for the bull, two-tenths for the ram,
one-tenth for each of the seven lambs.
Add a male goat as a sin offering — beyond the atonement sin offering, the daily burnt offering with its grain, and the drink offerings.
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, gather as a sacred assembly. Do no ordinary work. Celebrate a festival to the LORD for seven days.
Bring a burnt offering, a fire-offering, a fragrance that pleases the LORD: thirteen young bulls, two rams, fourteen year-old lambs — all without flaw.
With them, the grain offering: fine flour mixed with oil — three-tenths of an ephah for each of the thirteen bulls, two-tenths for each of the two rams,
one-tenth for each of the fourteen lambs.
Add a male goat as a sin offering — beyond the daily burnt offering with its grain and drink offering.
Second day: twelve young bulls, two rams, fourteen year-old lambs without flaw,
with grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs — measured by their number, by the rule.
And a male goat as a sin offering — beyond the daily burnt offering with its grain and drink offerings.
Third day: eleven bulls, two rams, fourteen year-old lambs without flaw,
with grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs — measured by their number, by the rule.
And a male goat as a sin offering — beyond the daily burnt offering with its grain and drink offering.
Fourth day: ten bulls, two rams, fourteen year-old lambs without flaw,
with grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs — measured by their number, by the rule.
And a male goat as a sin offering — beyond the daily burnt offering with its grain and drink offering.
Fifth day: nine bulls, two rams, fourteen year-old lambs without flaw,
with grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs — measured by their number, by the rule.
And a male goat as a sin offering — beyond the daily burnt offering with its grain and drink offering.
Sixth day: eight bulls, two rams, fourteen year-old lambs without flaw,
with grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs — measured by their number, by the rule.
And a male goat as a sin offering — beyond the daily burnt offering with its grain and drink offering.
Seventh day: seven bulls, two rams, fourteen year-old lambs without flaw,
with grain and drink offerings for the bulls, rams, and lambs — measured by their number, by the rule.
And a male goat as a sin offering — beyond the daily burnt offering with its grain and drink offering.
Eighth day: gather for a solemn assembly. Do no ordinary work.
Bring a burnt offering, a fire-offering, a fragrance that pleases the LORD: one bull, one ram, seven year-old lambs without flaw,
with grain and drink offerings for the bull, ram, and lambs — measured by their number, by the rule.
And a male goat as a sin offering — beyond the daily burnt offering with its grain and drink offering.

These are the offerings you present to the LORD at your appointed festivals — over and above whatever you bring as vows, freewill gifts, burnt offerings, grain offerings, drink offerings, or peace offerings.
Moses told the Israelites everything the LORD had commanded him.

com.d:
# Numbers 29: The Rhythm of Worship and Remember

The spiritual heart of Numbers 29 is this: God builds rhythms into our relationship with him, and faithful worship—both in the seasons of joy and in the regular, unmarked days—shapes a people prepared to follow him.

In this chapter, Moses outlines the sacred calendar of offerings for Israel's feasts and festivals throughout the year. From the Day of Atonement through the Feast of Tabernacles, each occasion carries specific sacrifices and assemblies. What strikes us is the remarkable consistency: morning and evening offerings continue unchanged; the prescribed animals, the grain, the wine all flow according to God's design. This wasn't meant to be burdensome but rather reassuring—a people could know where they stood with God because God had established the way.

We live in a culture suspicious of rhythm and routine. We prize spontaneity and often view repeated practices as hollow ritual. Yet Numbers 29 whispers something countercultural: there is profound grace in returning again and again to the same practices of worship. A daily rhythm of prayer, weekly gathering with God's people, annual moments of remembrance—these are not cages but pathways. They carry us through seasons when we feel alive and seasons when we feel numb. They anchor us when circumstances shift violently around us.

The beauty here is also in the particularities. God didn't prescribe vague "offerings" but exact numbers—two rams, fourteen lambs, specific measures of grain. This specificity says: your worship matters enough for God to be detailed about it. Your life isn't lost in abstraction; it's held in the concrete reality of a God who knows precisely where you are.

Consider the rhythms already shaping your spiritual life. What daily, weekly, or annual practices remind you that you belong to God? Where might God be inviting you to establish a new rhythm that would keep you close to his heart?
com.s:
Numbers 29 presents the culminating section of the festival calendar legislation that begins in chapter 28, detailing the public offerings required for the seventh month's sacred occasions—the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the eight-day Feast of Tabernacles. This chapter belongs to the Priestly source material and reflects the developed liturgical consciousness of Israel's cultic tradition, likely reaching its final form during or after the exilic period when precise ritual observance became paramount for maintaining communal identity.

The chapter opens with regulations for the first day of the seventh month, designated by the distinctive term *yom teruah* (יוֹם תְּרוּעָה), literally "a day of blowing" or "shouting." The noun *teruah* carries connotations of alarm, acclamation, and joyful noise, suggesting both warning and celebration. This occasion later developed into what rabbinic Judaism calls Rosh Hashanah. The tenth day's observances for the Day of Atonement emphasize self-denial through the phrase *te'annu et-nafshotekem* (תְּעַנּוּ אֶת־נַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם), "you shall afflict yourselves," traditionally understood as fasting and abstention.

The most striking feature of Numbers 29 is the elaborate sacrificial schema for Tabernacles (Sukkot), beginning on the fifteenth day. The offerings include a remarkable descending sequence of bulls: thirteen on the first day, twelve on the second, diminishing by one each day until seven bulls are offered on the seventh day, totaling seventy bulls across the week. Scholars have proposed various explanations for this pattern, including associations with the seventy nations tradition and cosmological symbolism related to the lunar calendar cycle.

The term *atseret* (עֲצֶרֶת), rendered "solemn assembly," designates the eighth day as a distinct closing festival requiring cessation from ordinary labor. This word derives from the root meaning "to restrain" or "to hold back," indicating a day of sacred restraint and gathering.

The meticulous quantification throughout—specifying exact numbers of bulls, rams, lambs, grain offerings, and drink offerings—reflects the Priestly concern that proper worship requires precise adherence to divine instruction. The cumulative effect presents Israel's liturgical year as reaching its crescendo in the seventh month, with Tabernacles serving as the agricultural and spiritual apex of communal celebration before Yahweh.
com.p:
Numbers 29 stands within the wilderness period, approximately 1400 years before the Incarnation, as Israel camped on the plains of Moab preparing to enter the Promised Land. This passage belongs to the era between Exodus and Kingdom, when God was forming a covenant people through law, sacrifice, and sacred calendar. Here Moses delivers the final instructions concerning the appointed feasts of the seventh month—the Feast of Trumpets, the Day of Atonement, and the Feast of Tabernacles—each carrying prophetic weight that stretches across the entire biblical narrative.

The seventh month opens with trumpet blasts on the first day, a day of sacred assembly and rest from ordinary labor. Prophetically, this feast awaits its ultimate fulfillment when the trumpet of God shall sound at Christ's return, gathering His elect from the four winds. Paul draws upon this imagery when declaring that "the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable." What Israel rehearsed annually in shadow, the church anticipates in substance.

Ten days later comes the Day of Atonement, the most solemn day of Israel's calendar, requiring affliction of soul and a sin offering for cleansing. This day found its definitive fulfillment when Christ, the true High Priest, entered not an earthly tabernacle but heaven itself, offering His own blood once for all. The book of Hebrews expounds this mystery: the repeated sacrifices of Levitical priests testified to their insufficiency, while Christ's single offering perfected forever those being sanctified. Yet an eschatological dimension remains—Zechariah prophesied that Israel will one day look upon Him whom they pierced and mourn, a national Day of Atonement still future.

The Feast of Tabernacles dominates this chapter with its elaborate eight-day celebration and remarkable sequence of diminishing bulls—seventy in total, representing the nations. This harvest feast commemorated wilderness wanderings while anticipating the ingathering of peoples to God. Its fulfillment unfolds in stages: Christ tabernacled among humanity at His first advent, the Spirit now tabernacles within believers, and at the consummation God will dwell with His people in the New Jerusalem where He wipes every tear away.

The sheer volume of sacrifices prescribed here—hundreds of animals—underscores both the gravity of sin and the costliness of redemption. Every burnt offering ascended as pleasing aroma, pointing forward to the one offering that would truly satisfy divine justice. The church now lives in the reality these feasts prefigured, yet still awaits their consummate fulfillment when shadow gives way completely to substance at Christ's glorious appearing.
